title: Wren and the Will
premise: Retired detective Emrys Lockridge, now barely keeping her failing bookshop afloat, receives two letters in the same week: one confessing to the Marrow Lane murder that ended her career twenty years ago, the other promising a third victim unless she reopens the case. The confessed killer, dying of illness and seeking absolution, insists the man hanged for the crime was innocent — and that the true murderer is someone Emrys trusted. As she digs through rotted case files and old loyalties, she discovers the second letter-writer is the real killer, still watching, still punishing those who knew the truth. Emrys must choose between turning the evidence over to a police force that once discarded her, or staging a dangerous private trap to force a confession — a choice that costs her the bookshop, an old friendship, and nearly her life, but finally closes the case that closed her.
about_author: Sebastian Eriksen is the pen name of a former small-town court reporter who spent a decade transcribing the gap between what witnesses saw and what they swore to. Wren and the Will is their third novel, written in a coastal house with too many bookshelves and one stubborn cat.

chapters.title: Two Envelopes, One Hand
chapters.summary: Emrys Lockridge, dusting the unsold shelves of her failing bookshop, opens two letters: a dying man's confession to the Marrow Lane murder, and an anonymous promise that 'the third is coming.' Her hands shake — she worked the original case. POV: Emrys. Beat: dread disguised as curiosity; the quiet life cracks open.

chapters.title: The Case That Closed Me
chapters.summary: Emrys recounts the 2003 Marrow Lane killing: a young woman strangled, a handyman convicted on Emrys's own testimony, her career ended shortly after by a scandal she never explained. She burns the first letter, then fishes it from the grate. POV: Emrys, with flashbacks. Beat: guilt resurfacing; she cannot let it go twice.

chapters.title: Confession of a Dying Man
chapters.summary: Emrys tracks the confessor, Arthur Pell, to a hospice in Grayhaven. Wasted and lucid, he admits he lied at trial — coached, paid, terrified — and swears the convicted man, Daniel Voss, hanged himself innocent. He gives her a name he never said aloud: 'Ask about the will.' POV: Emrys. Beat: the ground tilts.

chapters.title: Ask About the Will
chapters.summary: The victim, Clara Mowbray, left a will Emrys never knew existed — amending everything to a beneficiary days before her death. The solicitor who drafted it has since vanished from records. Emrys pulls her old case notes from a storage unit she swore she'd never open. POV: Emrys. Beat: obsession rekindling, fear of her own hunger for it.

chapters.title: The Second Letter Writer
chapters.summary: A third letter arrives — addressed to Emrys by name, describing her visit to Pell in detail. The writer knows her movements. It warns: 'Some doors are locked for your protection, Detective.' Emrys realizes she isn't investigating a cold case; she's being led through one. POV: Emrys. Beat: hunter realizing she's prey.

chapters.title: Voss's Sister
chapters.summary: Emrys finds Nell Voss, Daniel's sister, running a laundrette and hating her. Nell has spent twenty years collecting her own evidence and initially refuses to help — then sees Emrys's letters and goes pale: she's received them too. POV: Emrys, with Nell's guarded counterpoint. Beat: reluctant alliance; two women bound by the same wound.

chapters.title: What the Solicitor Knew
chapters.summary: Digging into the vanished solicitor, Gerald Hask, Emrys finds he liquidated his practice weeks after Clara's death and died in a boating 'accident' — ruled misadventure by a young constable named Rowan Pike, now the town's chief inspector. POV: Emrys. Beat: the conspiracy widens; the law itself is compromised.

chapters.title: An Old Wound, An Old Friend
chapters.summary: Emrys approaches her former partner, Frank Adeyemi, the one colleague who defended her during the scandal that ended her career. He begs her to drop it — the letters are bait, and whoever wrote them wants her ruined or dead. Their argument cracks something tender between them. POV: alternating Emrys and Frank. Beat: love against duty, first fracture.

chapters.title: The Scandal, Told Plainly
chapters.summary: Emrys finally confesses to Nell why her career ended: she was pressured to bury Hask's connection to the will, refused, and was framed for evidence tampering. She took the fall to protect Frank, who was being set up worse. POV: Emrys, unflinching. Beat: shame aired; the price of her integrity made explicit.

chapters.title: The Beneficiary
chapters.summary: The will's beneficiary traces back to Clara's employer, the late Aldous Mowbray — her uncle, it turns out, not her cousin, and the man whose 'grief' Emrys always found rehearsed. He died wealthy and respected. His estate passed to his son, Julian Mowbray, now a magistrate. POV: Emrys. Beat: the killer's shape emerging — powerful, protected, patient.

chapters.title: Watching the Watcher
chapters.summary: Emrys notices the same grey car outside her shop three nights running. She stages her flat to look abandoned and follows the car to Julian Mowbray's estate gates — where it parks, waits, and reports. Someone is surveilling her on Mowbray's behalf. POV: Emrys. Beat: cold fear hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: Pell's Last Statement
chapters.summary: Arthur Pell dies before Emrys can return, but the hospice nurse hands over a sealed statement he made for her: names, dates, and the payment trail from Mowbray's estate. Within a day, the statement is stolen from her shop — but Emrys had already photographed every page. POV: Emrys. Beat: loss and cunning in one breath; the trap closes both ways.

chapters.title: The Third Victim
chapters.summary: The hospice nurse is found dead — staged as a suicide, but with Clara Mowbray's signature ligature mark. The killer has resumed after twenty years, exactly as the second letter promised. Emrys carries the guilt of having led him to her. POV: Emrys, with a chilling brief interlude in the killer's POV, unnamed. Beat: grief, fury, and the stakes made mortal.

chapters.title: Pike's Bargain
chapters.summary: Chief Inspector Pike confronts Emrys: he knows she's investigating, and he knows what he ruled on Hask's death was wrong. He offers her a deal — bring him evidence against Mowbray and he'll reopen everything, including her scandal. But she must do it quietly, above him there are hands she can't see. POV: alternating Emrys and Pike. Beat: justice inside the law, offered at a price of trust.

chapters.title: Nell's File
chapters.summary: Nell finally reveals her own twenty-year file: letters Clara sent Daniel, proving they'd discovered Mowbray was abusing his position — and that Clara planned to expose him. The will was Clara's insurance. Mowbray killed her for it, then buried the paper trail. POV: Nell, then Emrys. Beat: the victim's voice recovered; the case turns from who to how to prove.

chapters.title: The Trap Is Baited
chapters.summary: Emrys leaks word that a surviving copy of Clara's letters will be 'authenticated' at her bookshop after hours. She, Nell, Frank, and Pike lay a private trap — outside the law, because the law inside Mowbray's reach can't be trusted. Frank objects; Emrys refuses to wait for another body. POV: Emrys. Beat: the moral line crossed deliberately; resolve at full burn.

chapters.title: Night at the Bookshop
chapters.summary: The trap springs — but not on Julian Mowbray. The intruder is his fixer, the grey-car driver, sent to burn the letters and Emrys with them. A violent struggle; Frank takes a knife meant for Emrys. Pike's team arrives late but takes the fixer alive. POV: Emrys, kinetic and terrified. Beat: climax's first edge; love bleeding literally.

chapters.title: The Man Behind the Magistrate
chapters.summary: The fixer, facing charges, trades up: he names Julian Mowbray as his employer for twenty years — silencing, paying, watching. But Mowbray is a magistrate with allies, and the evidence is circumstantial. Pike warns they have one shot before Mowbray's people scrub everything. POV: Emrys and Pike. Beat: victory that feels fragile; the system straining against its rot.

chapters.title: The Confession Recording
chapters.summary: Emrys requests a meeting with Mowbray as a private citizen — a woman selling the letters back. Wearing a wire provided by Pike, she provokes him with Clara's own words until he corrects her with the detail only the killer knows. He realizes too late; his allies move to protect him. POV: Emrys, taut. Beat: the climax — courage, terror, and a monster speaking plainly.

chapters.title: Arrest, and the Long Shadow
chapters.summary: Mowbray is arrested at his own courthouse steps. His allies begin falling — but so does the case against Emrys's old scandal, reopened and reversed, her name cleared twenty years too late to matter. Frank, recovering, asks why she never told him she took the fall for him. POV: alternating Emrys and Frank. Beat: justice outside and inside the law at once; grief and relief entangled.

chapters.title: What Survival Cost
chapters.summary: Emrys buries the nurse, visits Pell's grave, and sits with Nell in the laundrette as Daniel's conviction is formally posthumously quashed. Survival, she reflects, was never free — it cost her career, Frank's trust, and the illusion that walking away was possible. POV: Emrys, quiet. Beat: the price of survival tallied honestly, without bitterness.

chapters.title: The Last Letter
chapters.summary: A final letter arrives — from Julian Mowbray, awaiting trial, asking why she didn't let it stay closed. Emrys reads it once, then shelves it beside the others in the bookshop's back room, a small archive of the case that remade her. She repaints the shop sign, reopens the door, and lets the morning in. POV: Emrys. Beat: resolution — the case closed at last, and the woman who closed it, open again.
